Lessons.Title: Use a Protractor to Draw Angles
ExplanationParagraphs: 2021 original Grade 4 Unit 7 Lesson 11 — Use a Protractor to Draw Angles. Goal: construct specified angle measurements accurately using a protractor and ruler; then compare and verify another student's drawing. This is a construction lesson rather than a mere numerical angle identification task.

Source lesson timeline: Warm-up Estimation Exploration: Long Hand and Short Hand (10 min), Activity 1 Draw These Angles (15 min), Activity 2 Angles Made to Order (20 min), Synthesis (10 min), original publisher Cool-down A Ray or Two (5 min, teacher-login gated).

Warm-up source clock drawing: learners estimate too low/about right/too high. The ORIGINAL teacher guidance reveals an angular turn of 143°, traced clockwise from the hour hand to minute hand. This is a picture-specific estimate (NOT an exact-hour clock generated by the earlier U07:L07 family). Discuss estimates against 143°; actual picture remains original source artwork.

Activity 1: first draw a line neither vertical nor horizontal, mark a point, and construct a perpendicular line through it using a REAL protractor (no paper folding). The source teacher shows equivalent 90° alignments 0°→90°, 20°→110° on outer scale, or 40°→130° on inner scale: each difference is exactly 90°.

Activity 1 second student task: start at the source ray from M; add rays to make angles 40°, 20°, and 95° and label their measures. Find and label the resulting unlabelled REFLEX angle greater than 180°. The size varies because rays may be drawn above/below, adjacent/nested; the source teacher synthesis specifically says placing the 20° ray INSIDE the 40° angle can make the last reflex angle 20° larger than another arrangement. Do NOT invent a fixed answer or mark student drawing numeric data without examining the layout.

Activity 2: make four independently drawn angles on index cards labelled a–d; a: less than 35°; b: between 35° and 80°; c: greater than 80° and less than 120°; d: greater than 120° and less than 180°. Exchange cards, use a real protractor to measure and correct any out-of-range work, and KEEP cards for the next lesson U07:L12. Physical peer review is part of source scope.

Construct accurately: vertex at baseline ray endpoint; align protractor centre at vertex and zero with initial ray; mark the required tick on THAT zero-aligned scale; remove tool and draw ray through the mark; remeasure. Tool alignment/tick density can cause errors.

First-party Edulytics Cool-down (NOT the gated original A Ray or Two): use a protractor to DRAW an angle of 75°, label the vertex M, and show the teacher how the selected zero mark gives 75°. Retain paper image/teacher verification; numeric answer alone does not demonstrate construction.

Digital Practice: REUSE existing exact protractor-zero-scale reading family from U07:L09 and perpendicular judgement family from U07:L10 as supporting skills. They DO NOT digitally assess actual angle construction, range-constrained drawing cards, source clock image, or reflex drawings; those remain teacher-reviewed. No unnecessary new math engine.

KeyConcepts.Title: Construct a specified angle
KeyConcepts.Definition: The angle is the degree amount of turn between two rays with a common vertex, irrespective of ray length or page orientation.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Centre the protractor exactly at the vertex, align baseline with the starting ray and the correct zero, mark θ°, draw the second ray and remeasure.
KeyConcepts.Example: To draw 95° at M, set a first ray, start at the correct 0°, mark 95° and draw the ray.

KeyConcepts.Title: Perpendicular construction from a line
KeyConcepts.Definition: Supporting lines meet at a right (90°) angle.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Their protractor readings on the same scale differ by 90°, even if the first isn't at zero.

KeyConcepts.Title: Reflex angle depends on where the rays are drawn
KeyConcepts.Definition: A reflex angle is strictly more than 180° and less than 360°.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Find rays' actual angular positions first; the source 20°/40°/95° choices are not sufficient to infer one global number.
KeyConcepts.Example: Different valid nested/adjacent constructions can produce different reflex measures; teacher verifies the drawn arc.

KeyConcepts.Title: Draw angles in specified intervals
KeyConcepts.Definition: Source activity asks for four card drawings in given open numeric ranges.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Protractor-check each actual drawn angle and enforce card a <35°, b between 35° and 80°, c 80°<θ<120°, d 120°<θ<180°.
KeyConcepts.Example: Sample independently chosen values 25°, 55°, 100°, 145° satisfy a,b,c,d respectively.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source estimation clock angle
WorkedExamples.Question: Warm-up: estimate the clockwise turn from hour to minute hand as too low/about right/too high.
WorkedExamples.Method: Compare shown source picture with familiar 90° and 180° benchmarks.
Steps: Use the displayed clock and make three estimates.
Possible independent examples: 120° too low, 140° close, 160° too high.
WorkedExamples.Check: The 143° is source figure-specific, not an exact-hour clock benchmark.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original protractor perpendicular construction
WorkedExamples.Question: Draw a non-vertical, non-horizontal line and then one perpendicular line passing through point P.
WorkedExamples.Method: Keep centre on P and make a 90° angle with either direction of first line.
Steps: Draw a slanted straight line and mark P.
Align the protractor with the first straight line and centre with P.
On a common scale, mark a ray 90° away.
Draw the second full supporting line through P and verify four right angles.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Two perpendicular lines through P, teacher-reviewed.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original specified rays at point M
WorkedExamples.Question: Given ray from M, draw and label 40°, 20° and 95° angles.
WorkedExamples.Method: Place protractor centre at M, one scale's zero at source initial ray, and choose appropriate ray positions.
Steps: Place M at the protractor centre and the initial ray on baseline.
Draw rays through the 40°, 20°, 95° marks chosen in your orientation.
Label degree sizes and identify any remaining reflex angle with an arc.
Observe actual ray placement before computing the remaining turn.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Three constructed target angles, plus a REFLEX value dependent on the drawing.
WorkedExamples.Check: No fixed numeric answer for the reflex angle claimed; source teacher says arrangements differ.

WorkedExamples.Title: Four source card interval checks
WorkedExamples.Question: On cards a–d, produce an angle meeting each interval.
WorkedExamples.Method: Independently choose target values strictly within each range, construct and then remeasure.
Steps: Swap cards and independently measure and correct partner work.
WorkedExamples.Answer: One possible valid set 25°, 55°, 100°, 145°; many sets allowed.
WorkedExamples.Check: The card drawings require a real protractor, not merely numerical interval matching.

WorkedExamples.Title: Edulytics independent Cool-down
WorkedExamples.Question: Use a protractor to construct a 75° angle at vertex M, and verify it.
WorkedExamples.Method: Draw baseline, align zero, mark 75° and create the second ray.
Steps: Draw a ray with labelled endpoint M.
Place the centre at M and align zero with the ray.
Make the 75° mark on the aligned scale, draw the second ray and check with a real protractor.
WorkedExamples.Answer: A constructed angle measuring 75° with vertex M, teacher-confirmed.
WorkedExamples.Check: Not a copy of the protected publisher Cool-down.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming the 143° source clock angle is an exact whole-hour 30° multiple.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source illustration/teacher answer is 143°, not an exact-hour clock family case.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Estimate the actual source clock drawing and compare to the instructor's 143° reveal.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Putting the protractor centre beside rather than ON the ray's vertex.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: This shifts the constructed angle relative to the intended origin.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Align centre on M and the starting ray on the proper zero baseline before marking degrees.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Computing the unspecified reflex angle from 20°+40°+95° without knowing ray layout.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Source permits drawing 20° inside or adjacent to 40°, changing remaining reflex measurement.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Inspect where the rays were actually constructed and use the resulting directed positions to compute the reflex.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Keeping inaccurate partner cards or interpreting a range as one fixed measure.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Source asks four open degree intervals and verification of independent drawings.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Choose and physically verify any permitted value, correct failures and save all four labelled cards for next lesson.

SummaryPoints: Source goal: construct angles of given measurements using protractor, not only read printed measures.
143° from the original clock warm-up is a teacher-revealed picture-specific angle.
Source instructions: perpendicular through slanted line; rays of 40°, 20°, 95° from M; compute remaining reflex from actual layout only.
Four labelled cards a–d require <35°, (35°,80°), (80°,120°), (120°,180°); swap, measure and save for next lesson.
Independent 75° construction Cool-down is teacher-scored, unlike numeric protractor scale Practice.
Reuse prior exact protractor and perpendicular numerical support families; Stage C test methods authored unrun.
